questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{3-5{e}^{2t}} & =L{3}+L{-5{e}^{2t}} \\  & =3L{1}-5L{{e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

$$
L{1}=\frac{1}{s},\,s>0
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =3L{1}-5L{{e}^{2t}} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{s}-5\cdot \frac{1}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{5}{s-2} \\  & =\frac{3(s-2)-5s}{s(s-2)} \\  & =-\frac{2(s+3)}{s(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{1}$ is defined for $s\in (0,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{2t}}$ is defined for $s\in (2,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(0,\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=(2,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>2.$

$$

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k

$$

$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}+{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4},\,s>4 \\ L{{e}^{-4t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4},\,s>-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{1}{s+4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4)+(s-4)}{(s-4)(s+4)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-16}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}-{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{3\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-3\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-3\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+3\text{i})-(s-3\text{i})}{(s-3\text{i})(s+3\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{6\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

questions.problem:
Given that for $s>\omega ,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)$ for $s>8.$
questions.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =L{4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+L{3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega , \\ L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(\omega t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>\omega .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8 \\ L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} & =\frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64},\,s>8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =4L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(8t)}+3L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(8t)} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}-64}+3\cdot \frac{8}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}-64}+\frac{24}{{s}^{2}-64} \\  & =\frac{4s+24}{{s}^{2}-64}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}$ for $s>5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}-{e}^{5t}} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}+L{-{e}^{5t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{5t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3 \\ L{{e}^{5t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5},\,s>5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-3t}}-L{{e}^{5t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3}-\frac{1}{s-5} \\  & =\frac{(s-5)-(s+3)}{(s+3)(s-5)} \\  & =\frac{-8}{(s+3)(s-5)} \\  & =-\frac{8}{(s+3)(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{5t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (5,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(-3,\infty) \cap (5,\infty) = (5,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 5.$

canonical_examples.problem: Use the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
\mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
\mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\sinh(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}-\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{3}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty)$ and $\mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty),$ we have that $\mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),
$$

that is, $s > 3.$
